explanations.answer: Divorcing a wife for any reason
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The Pharisees ask, "Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any reason?" (Matthew 19:3). Pharisees were a strict religious group, and Matthew says they came to test Him. So the question wasn't really about learning anything.

Good guess, friend, because taxes did come up in a test question on another day. That's Matthew 22:17, when the Pharisees ask whether it's lawful to pay the census tax to Caesar, the Roman emperor. Here in chapter 19, though, the test is about divorce. The question is whether a man may divorce his wife for any reason (Matthew 19:3).

Healing on the Sabbath did cause a stir in other places, like Matthew 12:10. Not here, though. In this passage Jesus heals the crowds (Matthew 19:2), and the Pharisees' question is about a man divorcing his wife for any reason (Matthew 19:3). Easy one to mix up when the Pharisees keep showing up with questions.

explanations.answer: When the Creator made them male and female
explanations.explanation: Right on, baker. Jesus says, "Have you not read that from the beginning the Creator 'made them male and female,'" (Matthew 19:4). He doesn't start with a rule. He starts at the beginning. These are people who know their Scriptures, so I think that question lands with a little sting.

Abraham, the father of Israel's people, did leave his homeland when God called him (Genesis 12:1). But Jesus doesn't go there. He says "from the beginning," and that takes Him all the way back to when the Creator "made them male and female" (Matthew 19:4). That's way before Abraham packed a single bag.

explanations.answer: When David became king of Israel
explanations.explanation: David was a great king, no doubt about it. But Jesus isn't pointing to a throne here. He says "from the beginning," which goes back to when the Creator "made them male and female" (Matthew 19:4). David shows up many, many chapters later in the story.

Yes, baker. Jesus says, "Therefore what God has joined together, let man not separate." (Matthew 19:6). He had just said they are no longer two, but one flesh. The line is short and it needs no help from me.

Nice try, friend, but no committee shows up in this verse. Jesus says, "Therefore what God has joined together, let man not separate." (Matthew 19:6). Nobody here is asked to approve a thing. The verse is about what God has joined.

A blessing from the priests sounds sweet, but that's not what Jesus says. He says, "Therefore what God has joined together, let man not separate." (Matthew 19:6). The focus is on what God has joined together and on man not separating it. Priests don't come up in the verse at all.

That's it, baker. Jesus says, "Moses permitted you to divorce your wives because of your hardness of heart." (Matthew 19:8). Notice He says Moses permitted it. He didn't say it was the plan. Then He adds, "But it was not this way from the beginning."

I get why it sounds nice, friend, but it's the opposite of what Jesus says. He says, "Moses permitted you to divorce your wives because of your hardness of heart." (Matthew 19:8). So the word is hardness, not purity. A hard heart is no help when you're working with dough or anything else.

Gladness is a lovely word, but it doesn't fit this verse. Jesus says, "Moses permitted you to divorce your wives because of your hardness of heart." (Matthew 19:8). That's a heavy line, and I think it's meant to be. The right word is hardness.

Careful, friend, this one flips on you. Jesus says the opposite: "But it was not this way from the beginning." (Matthew 19:8). Moses permitted divorce because of hardness of heart, but from the beginning the Creator made them male and female (Matthew 19:4). So divorce was not how it started.

Yes, baker. Jesus says, "Moses permitted you to divorce your wives because of your hardness of heart. But it was not this way from the beginning." (Matthew 19:8). So divorce was not the way it was from the beginning. He points them back to how things started, with the Creator making them male and female (Matthew 19:4).

That's right, baker. His disciples say, "If this is the case between a man and his wife, it is better not to marry." (Matthew 19:10). Jesus's teaching hit them hard. I think they were stunned, and honestly, I'd have been staring at my apron too.

This one is true, friend. After hearing Jesus, the disciples say, "If this is the case between a man and his wife, it is better not to marry." (Matthew 19:10). They said it out loud, right there. Jesus then answers, "Not everyone can accept this word, but only those to whom it has been given." (Matthew 19:11).

Yes, baker. Jesus says some "live like eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven." (Matthew 19:12). He names three kinds: those born that way, those made that way by men, and those who live that way for the kingdom. Then He says, "The one who can accept this should accept it."

The temple was the center of worship in Jerusalem, so I see why you picked it. But Jesus doesn't say that here. He says some live like eunuchs "for the sake of the kingdom of heaven." (Matthew 19:12). The temple never comes up in this passage.

Moses did just come up in this conversation, so that's a fair thought. The Pharisees asked about his order on divorce (Matthew 19:7). But when Jesus talks about those who live like eunuchs, He says it's "for the sake of the kingdom of heaven." (Matthew 19:12). The kingdom is the reason He gives.

explanations.answer: Let them come and do not hinder them
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Jesus says, "Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them!" (Matthew 19:14). The disciples had just rebuked the people bringing them. Jesus says the opposite, and He says it with an exclamation point.

explanations.answer: Let them wait until I finish teaching
explanations.explanation: Waiting sounds reasonable, friend, but Jesus never says it. He says, "Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them!" (Matthew 19:14). He doesn't put them on hold. I like that He says come, not later.

explanations.answer: Let them go home and come back later
explanations.explanation: That would've made the disciples happy, I bet. But Jesus says, "Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them!" (Matthew 19:14). Nobody gets sent home in this scene. The children are welcome to come to Him.
Yes, baker. Jesus says, "For the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these." (Matthew 19:14). That's His reason for not hindering the children. They are the ones He points to.

Close, because the people bringing them did the work of getting there. But Jesus says, "For the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these." (Matthew 19:14). He's pointing at the children themselves. The ones carrying them aren't the ones He names.

Teachers do a lot of good, friend, but they aren't who Jesus names here. He says, "For the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these." (Matthew 19:14). He's talking about the little children. No teachers are mentioned in this scene.

That's right, baker. Matthew says, "And after He had placed His hands on them, He went on from there." (Matthew 19:15). The children came for a touch and a prayer (Matthew 19:13), and they got it. The disciples' scolding didn't get the last word.

This one is true, friend. Matthew says, "And after He had placed His hands on them, He went on from there." (Matthew 19:15). The people brought the children so Jesus could place His hands on them and pray (Matthew 19:13). He did, and then He moved on.
